title: Edgar Battle and the Jack Hoxie show; study with James H. Wilson in Huntsville
summary: Jones praises Edgar Battle as bandleader of Jack Hoxie's show, then describes studying at A and M in Huntsville with cornetist James H. Wilson.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: of the band, but nobody had ever led. Jack Hoxey was a terrific cowboy like the Tom Mix here. But he had the One-O-One Ranch and who was the head bandmaster was Edgar Battle, a black man, not a white man. This was something that the Jet, Ebony, and the Pittsburgh Courier and nobody ever wrote about, because he only got - when he got to New Orleans he got writeups in the Picayune. When he got to Cincinnati it was the Cincinnati Inquirer. They said Edgar Battle; they didn't say black man. They said Edgar Battle. Edgar Battle stayed in all premier hotels before the advent of Civil Rights. Here I am and I was running around and I was going to Switzerland to go with Walter Young as a small unit but I wasn't allowed to go. I deviated myself to some ways and somehow or other I wound up at the A and M Institute in Huntsville, Alabama. Right on the outskirts 4 miles away is a place called Normal, Alabama, and at that time there was one of the greatest, foremost cornetists in the whole world. His name was James H. Wilson, because (who) Walter Crill worked on the Chautauqua shows was supposed to be America's foremost cornetist but Mr. James H. Wilson was the only one that could play the cadenza of a tune called "Salute Polka" and "Nelly Bly" also. He was the only one. That's when I began to get my musical education. I used to go -

Of course I played with Mr. Wilson but however when I went into the band room and he put up "Poet and Peasant" it took me two months to get back into the room. I didn't know nothing about a half note or less.
